label: The CMOS process flow
lesson:
# The CMOS process flow

A chip is built by repeating a small set of unit operations several hundred times on a silicon wafer: deposit a film, pattern it with lithography, etch or implant through the pattern, clean, and sometimes polish. The order of these modules is the process flow. A tool designer needs the flow because every layer in a layout is an instruction to one of these modules, and every design rule exists because some step in that sequence cannot do better.

## Modules repeated in a fixed order

A patterning module is lithography to define a shape in photoresist, then an etch, implant or deposition that transfers it, then resist strip and clean. A leading-edge logic flow repeats such modules for dozens of mask layers. They run in three phases. The front end of line (FEOL) builds transistors: isolation trenches, wells, gate stack, spacers, source and drain. The middle of line (MOL) builds the local contacts to source, drain and gate. The back end of line (BEOL) builds the stack of copper wiring levels and vias. The order is forced by temperature: dopant activation needs about 1000 C, while finished metal and low-k films survive only about 400 C, so devices come first and wiring last.

## From drawn layers to process steps

The layout a designer hands over is a set of planar masks. The active (diffusion) layer defines where shallow trench isolation is not etched, and therefore where transistors may exist. The poly or gate layer defines gate lines; a gate-cut layer later severs them. Implant layers select which regions receive well, threshold or source-drain doping, which is why each threshold-voltage flavour is a separate layer with its own spacing rules. Contact and via layers define holes, and metal layers define trenches to be filled with copper. Each drawn layer therefore inherits the limits of its module: the resolution of its lithography, the selectivity of its etch, the conformality of its fill.

## What the flow hides from the layout

Many steps have no drawn layer: spacer deposition, epitaxial source-drain growth, silicide, dummy-gate replacement in gate-last flows, chemical-mechanical polishing, selective depositions. They still shape the final geometry and electrical behaviour. A via-to-gate short depends on film thicknesses and etch depths that the 2D layout cannot show. These undrawn steps reach design tools indirectly, through design rules, technology files and parasitic extraction models. For this reason a rule that looks arbitrary in two dimensions often has a three-dimensional cause, and a tool designer who knows the flow can tell which rules are fundamental and which might be relaxed by a DTCO study.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology: Fundamentals, Practice and Modeling", chapters 1 and 2; Sze and Lee, "Semiconductor Devices: Physics and Technology", the chapters on processing.

label: Silicon wafers and substrates
lesson:
# Silicon wafers and substrates

Every chip starts as a slice of a single silicon crystal. Wafer diameter, orientation and substrate type are fixed before any design exists, yet they decide how many dies a fab can make per wafer, how much area is lost at the edge, and which transistor structures are available. For a tool designer, the wafer is the domain over which yield and cost are computed, and its geometry is the first input to every dies-per-wafer and cost model.

## From crystal to wafer

Electronic-grade silicon is melted and pulled as a single crystal ingot from a seed by the Czochralski process. The ingot is ground to a precise diameter, sliced, lapped, etched and polished to a mirror finish. Logic wafers today are 300 mm in diameter and about 775 um thick; 200 mm and smaller wafers remain common for analog, power and older nodes. The surface is cut along a crystal plane, usually (100) for CMOS, because orientation sets oxide interface quality and carrier mobility. Wafer area is $\pi r^2$: a 300 mm wafer has radius 15 cm and area $\pi \times 15^2 \approx 706.9$ square cm, so a lot of 25 wafers carries about 17,671 square cm of silicon.

## Edge exclusion and usable area

The outer few millimetres of a wafer are unreliable: films are thinner, the edge is bevelled, and handling and clamping damage it. Fabs define an edge exclusion inside which no product die may sit. The usable disc has radius $r - e$, so the fraction lost is $1 - ((r - e)/r)^2$. For a 300 mm wafer with a 3 mm exclusion, $1 - (147/150)^2 = 3.96\%$ of the area is gone before a single die is placed. Because the ring has fixed width, it costs a small wafer proportionally more: the same 3 mm takes $1 - (97/100)^2 = 5.91\%$ of a 200 mm wafer.

## Substrate choices and wafer size

Beyond bulk silicon, a fab can start from an epitaxial wafer, a lightly doped crystalline layer grown on a heavily doped substrate to suppress latch-up, or a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer, a thin silicon film on a buried oxide. Fully depleted SOI gives good electrostatics and back-gate biasing without fins, which changes the device models and some layout rules in the PDK. Moving to a larger wafer raises usable area by the square of the radius ratio: going from 200 mm to 300 mm with a 3 mm exclusion multiplies usable area by $(147/97)^2 = 2.297$, while processing cost per wafer grows less, which is why each transition cut cost per die.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 3 on crystal growth and wafer preparation.

label: Thermal oxidation and the Deal-Grove model
lesson:
# Thermal oxidation and the Deal-Grove model

Heating silicon in oxygen or steam grows silicon dioxide that is consumed from the wafer itself. Thermal oxide was the gate dielectric for decades and still forms interface layers, pad oxides and isolation liners. The Deal-Grove model predicts its thickness from time and temperature with one quadratic equation. It is also the first model a process simulator implements, and it shows how a diffusion-limited process slows down as it proceeds.

## Oxide grows into the silicon

Oxidation converts silicon into SiO2, and the oxide occupies more volume than the silicon it replaces. For every nanometre of oxide grown, about 0.44 nm of silicon is consumed, so 44% of the oxide lies below the original silicon surface and 56% above it. Growing 100 nm of oxide eats 44 nm of silicon. This matters for geometry: features defined in silicon before oxidation shrink, and a step in the silicon surface reappears in the oxide. Dry oxygen grows dense, slow oxide suited to thin, high-quality layers; steam (wet oxidation) grows several times faster and is used for thicker films.

## The Deal-Grove equation

Oxidant must diffuse through the existing oxide and then react at the silicon interface. Balancing those two fluxes gives $x^2 + A x = B (t + \tau)$, where $x$ is oxide thickness, $B$ is the parabolic rate constant, $B/A$ the linear rate constant and $\tau$ accounts for oxide already present. Solve the quadratic: $x = \left(-A + \sqrt{A^2 + 4B(t+\tau)}\right)/2$. With $A = 0.2$ um, $B = 0.1$ um^2/h, $\tau = 0$ and $t = 2$ h: $x = (-0.2 + \sqrt{0.04 + 0.8})/2 = 0.358$ um, which is 358 nm.

## Linear and parabolic regimes

For thin oxides, $x^2 \ll A x$ and growth is linear: $x \approx (B/A)(t + \tau)$, limited by the interface reaction. For thick oxides, $x^2 \gg A x$ and $x \approx \sqrt{B t}$, limited by diffusion through the oxide. To find the time for a target thickness, rearrange: $t = (x^2 + A x)/B - \tau$. With $A = 0.2$ um and $B = 0.1$ um^2/h, 0.5 um needs $(0.25 + 0.1)/0.1 = 3.5$ h. Doubling the target to 1 um needs $(1 + 0.2)/0.1 = 12$ h, more than three times as long. The classic model is known to underpredict the fast initial growth of very thin dry oxides, which is why thin gate interfaces are calibrated separately.

## Going deeper

Deal and Grove, "General Relationship for the Thermal Oxidation of Silicon", Journal of Applied Physics (1965); Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 6.

label: Dopant diffusion and thermal budget
prereqs: Heat equation and separation of variables
lesson:
# Dopant diffusion and thermal budget

Dopants placed by implantation do not stay put. Every hot step afterwards lets them spread by diffusion, which moves junctions, widens doped regions and shortens effective channel length. The process engineer tracks a thermal budget: the accumulated product of diffusivity and time. A tool designer meets this through device models, short-channel behaviour and through why advanced flows use fast spike and laser anneals rather than long furnace bakes.

## Fick's law and the diffusion length

Dopant flux follows Fick's first law, $J = -D\, \partial C/\partial x$, and mass conservation gives the diffusion equation $\partial C/\partial t = D\, \partial^2 C/\partial x^2$, the same equation as heat flow. Its solutions spread over a characteristic length $2\sqrt{Dt}$. A fixed dose diffusing from a thin surface layer becomes a Gaussian with standard deviation $\sqrt{2Dt}$; a constant surface concentration gives a complementary error function profile. With $D = 1 \times 10^{-14}$ cm^2/s and a 60-minute anneal, $Dt = 3.6 \times 10^{-11}$ cm^2, $\sqrt{Dt} = 6 \times 10^{-6}$ cm, and $2\sqrt{Dt} = 120$ nm.

## Arrhenius temperature dependence

Diffusivity depends steeply on temperature: $D = D_0 e^{-E_a/kT}$, with activation energies of roughly 3 to 4 eV for common dopants in silicon and $k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K. The ratio between two temperatures is $D_2/D_1 = \exp[(E_a/k)(1/T_1 - 1/T_2)]$. For $E_a = 3.5$ eV, going from 900 C (1173 K) to 1000 C (1273 K) gives $1/T_1 - 1/T_2 = 6.70 \times 10^{-5}$ per K, times $3.5/8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ is 2.72, and the ratio is $e^{2.72} \approx 15$. A hundred degrees changes diffusion by more than an order of magnitude.

## Adding up the thermal budget

Successive anneals add their $Dt$ products when the dopant and its diffusion mechanism are the same: total $Dt = \sum_i D_i t_i$, and the final spread is $2\sqrt{\sum D_i t_i}$. A 10 s spike at $5 \times 10^{-14}$ cm^2/s contributes $5 \times 10^{-13}$ cm^2; a 300 s anneal at $2 \times 10^{-15}$ cm^2/s contributes $6 \times 10^{-13}$ cm^2; together $2\sqrt{1.1 \times 10^{-12}} = 21$ nm. This is why later steps run cold: any heat after the source-drain implant moves junctions that set channel length. Real dopants also show transient enhanced diffusion after implant damage, which a simple constant-$D$ budget understates.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 7; Crank, "The Mathematics of Diffusion".

label: Ion implantation profiles
lesson:
# Ion implantation profiles

Ion implantation shoots ionized dopant atoms into the wafer at a chosen energy and dose. It sets wells, threshold adjustments, halos, extensions and source-drain regions, each through its own mask layer. To first order the implanted atoms form a Gaussian in depth. That one model gives peak concentration, the doping at any depth and the junction depth, which are the numbers device and process simulators start from.

## Dose, range and the Gaussian profile

An implant is specified by species, energy and dose $Q$, the number of ions per square centimetre. Energy sets the projected range $R_p$, the mean depth, and the straggle $\Delta R_p$, the standard deviation of depth. The profile is $N(x) = N_p \exp\left(-(x - R_p)^2 / 2\Delta R_p^2\right)$. Integrating it over depth must return the dose, so the peak is $N_p = Q/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\Delta R_p)$. For $Q = 1 \times 10^{15}$ cm^-2 and $\Delta R_p = 20$ nm $= 2 \times 10^{-6}$ cm, $N_p = 10^{15}/(2.507 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}) = 1.99 \times 10^{20}$ cm^-3.

## Concentration at a given depth

Once $N_p$ is known, the concentration at depth $x$ follows from the distance to the peak in units of straggle. At one straggle from the peak the factor is $e^{-1/2} = 0.607$; at two straggles, $e^{-2} = 0.135$; at three, $e^{-4.5} = 0.011$. Take $N_p = 2 \times 10^{20}$ cm^-3, $R_p = 50$ nm and $\Delta R_p = 20$ nm. At $x = 80$ nm the depth is 1.5 straggles from the peak, so $N = 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1.125} = 6.49 \times 10^{19}$ cm^-3. Real profiles are skewed and have channelling tails, so production simulators use Pearson distributions or Monte Carlo, but the Gaussian is the shape to reason with.

## Junction depth

The metallurgical junction sits where the implanted concentration equals the background doping $N_B$ of the opposite type. Solving $N(x_j) = N_B$ beyond the peak gives $x_j = R_p + \Delta R_p \sqrt{2 \ln(N_p/N_B)}$. With $N_p = 2 \times 10^{20}$, $N_B = 1 \times 10^{17}$ cm^-3, $R_p = 50$ nm and $\Delta R_p = 20$ nm: $\ln(2000) = 7.60$, $\sqrt{15.2} = 3.90$, so $x_j = 50 + 78 = 128$ nm. The logarithm makes junction depth insensitive to dose but linear in straggle, which is why shallow junctions need low energies, heavy ions and minimal later diffusion.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 8; Ziegler's SRIM documentation for range tables.

lesson:
# Epitaxy and strained layers

Epitaxy grows a crystalline film that continues the lattice of the crystal beneath it. Modern transistors depend on it: raised source and drain regions, silicon-germanium channels and stressors, and the alternating Si and SiGe stack from which gate-all-around nanosheets are released. A tool designer meets epitaxy through strain-dependent device models, merged source-drain regions in extraction, and spacing rules around fins and sheets.

## Single-crystal growth on a template

In epitaxy, precursor gases such as silane or dichlorosilane, plus germane or dopant gases, decompose at the hot surface and the atoms settle into lattice sites continuing the substrate crystal. The result is single-crystal rather than polycrystalline or amorphous. Selective epitaxy is tuned so growth nucleates only on exposed silicon and not on oxide or nitride, which lets a flow grow source and drain only in the cavities beside the gates. In situ doping during growth reaches high active concentrations without implant damage. Gate-all-around flows start with an epitaxial superlattice of alternating Si and SiGe layers; the SiGe is later etched away selectively to leave stacked silicon sheets.

## Lattice mismatch and strain

Germanium's lattice constant is 5.658 angstrom against 5.431 for silicon. By Vegard's law, $\mathrm{Si}_{1-x}\mathrm{Ge}_x$ has $a \approx 5.431 + 0.227x$ angstrom. The mismatch with a silicon substrate is $f = (a_{film} - a_{sub})/a_{sub}$. For $x = 0.3$: $a = 5.499$ angstrom and $f = 0.068/5.431 = 1.25\%$. A thin film that stays pseudomorphic adopts the substrate's in-plane spacing, so a SiGe film on silicon is under compression. Strain is a design tool: compressive stress in the channel raises hole mobility, so PMOS source-drain regions use SiGe, while NMOS benefits from tensile stress.

## Critical thickness and layout consequences

Strain energy grows with film thickness. Past the critical thickness it becomes cheaper for the film to relax by forming misfit dislocations, which destroy the benefit and can short junctions; higher germanium content lowers that limit. Strain also depends on geometry: a stressor relaxes near free edges, so mobility depends on active length and on distance to diffusion breaks, effects that PDK models capture as layout-dependent parameters. Laterally overgrown epitaxy on adjacent fins can merge, changing source-drain resistance and parasitic capacitance, so extraction and spacing rules must know whether neighbouring fins merge.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter on epitaxy; Matthews and Blakeslee on misfit dislocations and critical thickness.

label: CVD, PVD and ALD
lesson:
# CVD, PVD and ALD

Most layers in a chip are deposited films: dielectrics between wires, barriers and seeds for copper, spacers that set feature widths, high-k gate dielectrics and work-function metals. Three families dominate, and each has a different conformality, thickness control and throughput. A tool designer cares because these properties set minimum widths, spacings and aspect ratios in the rules, and because in self-aligned patterning a film's thickness becomes a printed dimension.

## Three ways to put down a film

Chemical vapour deposition (CVD) reacts gas-phase precursors at or near a heated surface; plasma-enhanced CVD lowers the temperature so it can run in the back end. It is fast and fairly conformal. Physical vapour deposition (PVD), mainly sputtering, knocks atoms off a solid target with argon ions; they fly in nearly straight lines, so the flux is directional. It deposits metals such as barrier and seed layers. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) alternates two precursors, each of whose surface reactions saturates after one monolayer, so each cycle adds a fixed, small thickness regardless of local flux.

## ALD cycles and step coverage

Because ALD is self-limiting, thickness is cycles times growth per cycle (GPC). A 2.0 nm high-k layer at 0.1 nm per cycle needs 20 cycles; at 0.12 nm per cycle it needs $\lceil 16.7 \rceil = 17$. Conformality is measured by step coverage: film thickness on a trench bottom or sidewall divided by thickness on the open field. ALD reaches nearly 100%. CVD varies with chemistry and pressure. PVD in a high-aspect-ratio via can fall to a small fraction, because the bottom sees only a narrow cone of the incoming flux. If a PVD film is 20 nm on the field and 7 nm on the bottom, step coverage is 35%.

## Choosing a method by what the layer must do

A gate dielectric about two nanometres thick wrapped around a fin needs sub-angstrom control and full coverage, so it is ALD. Spacers in self-aligned double patterning become the final line width, so they need conformal, uniform ALD or CVD. A micrometre of inter-layer oxide would take thousands of ALD cycles, so it uses plasma CVD. PVD barriers overhang at the top of narrow openings and can pinch off before fill, leaving voids. These limits travel into design as rules on minimum trench width, spacing and aspect ratio. A fill process with poor conformality is one reason a foundry forbids certain narrow gaps.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 9 on thin-film deposition; George, "Atomic Layer Deposition: An Overview", Chemical Reviews (2010).

label: Etching: anisotropy, selectivity and over-etch
lesson:
# Etching: anisotropy, selectivity and over-etch

Etching transfers a lithographic pattern into the film below by removing exposed material. Its directionality, its selectivity to the mask and underlying layers, and the over-etch needed to clear thickness variation decide how faithfully the drawn shape becomes a physical one. Many design rules, from minimum spacing to enclosure and end-of-line margins, are etch rules in disguise, and etch bias is one of the effects OPC must model.

## Isotropic and anisotropic etch

Wet chemical etches remove material at the same rate in every direction: they are isotropic and undercut the mask by about the etch depth. Plasma, or reactive ion etching, combines reactive radicals with ions accelerated toward the wafer, and sidewall passivation protects vertical faces, so material is removed mainly downward. Anisotropy is $A = 1 - r_{lat}/r_{vert}$. A wet etch has $A = 0$; a plasma etch removing 300 nm/min vertically and 9 nm/min laterally has $A = 1 - 9/300 = 0.97$. Nanometre features with vertical sidewalls need $A$ very close to 1, which is why critical layers use plasma etch.

## Over-etch and etch time

A film is never perfectly uniform across a wafer, and etch rate varies too. To be sure every region clears, the recipe runs past the nominal endpoint by an over-etch, often 10 to 50 percent. The total time is $t = (h/r)(1 + OE)$. A 200 nm film at 250 nm/min takes 48 s nominally; with 30% over-etch it runs 62.4 s. During over-etch, the regions that cleared first are attacking the layer below, so the next number that matters is selectivity. Endpoint detection, which watches plasma emission for the moment the film clears, lets recipes keep over-etch as short as the uniformity allows.

## Selectivity and mask budget

Selectivity is the ratio of etch rates of the target film to another material, such as the mask or the stop layer below. A mask must survive the whole etch: consumed mask thickness is the equivalent film etched divided by selectivity. Etching 200 nm with 30% over-etch through a mask with 10:1 selectivity consumes $260/10 = 26$ nm of mask. Low selectivity forces thicker resist or hard masks, and thick resist limits resolution and aspect ratio. Etch also has pattern dependence: narrow openings etch more slowly than wide ones (aspect-ratio-dependent etching, or RIE lag), and dense and isolated features etch differently, effects that feed OPC models and density rules.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 10; Lieberman and Lichtenberg, "Principles of Plasma Discharges and Materials Processing".

label: Chemical-mechanical polishing and density
lesson:
# Chemical-mechanical polishing and density

Chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) flattens the wafer after deposition so that the next lithography step stays in focus, and it defines damascene copper lines by removing excess metal. Its removal rate depends on the local pattern density, so a layout's density map is a process input. This is why design rules impose minimum and maximum density in every window, and why fill tools insert dummy shapes.

## Preston's law

A rotating pad with an abrasive, chemically active slurry presses on the wafer. Removal rate follows Preston's empirical law, $RR = K_p P v$, proportional to applied pressure $P$ and relative velocity $v$, with $K_p$ capturing slurry chemistry and pad properties. Scaling from a known operating point needs no $K_p$: a step that removes 200 nm/min at 20 kPa and 1.0 m/s should remove $200 \times (25 \times 1.2)/(20 \times 1.0) = 300$ nm/min at 25 kPa and 1.2 m/s. Real processes deviate at low pressure and when chemistry dominates, but Preston's law is the model a CMP simulator starts from.

## Pattern density sets local removal

On a patterned wafer the pad touches raised features first. If a region has pattern density $\rho$, the fraction of area that is raised, the pressure on the raised parts is about $P/\rho$, so they polish at the blanket rate divided by $\rho$. The time to remove a step of height $h$ is $t = h \rho / K$, where $K$ is the blanket rate. At 200 nm/min blanket, a 400 nm step clears in 0.6 min at density 0.3 but in 1.6 min at density 0.8. Regions of different density therefore finish at different times and end up at different heights. In copper CMP the same physics produces dishing of wide lines and erosion of dense arrays.

## Density rules and dummy fill

To keep the post-CMP surface within the lithography focus budget, foundries require metal density between a minimum and maximum in every window, often tens of micrometres on a side and stepped across the die. If a 50 um by 50 um window must reach 25% density and holds 400 um^2 of metal, it needs $0.25 \times 2500 - 400 = 225$ um^2 of fill. Fill tools add floating or tied dummy shapes, which adds coupling capacitance to nearby signals, so timing-aware fill keeps dummies away from critical nets. Extraction must see the fill, or timing will be optimistic.

label: Lithographic resolution
lesson:
# Lithographic resolution

Lithography projects a mask pattern onto photoresist through a lens, and the finest pattern it can print sets the pitch of every critical layer. The Rayleigh relation ties that limit to wavelength, numerical aperture and a process factor $k_1$. A tool designer uses it to see why a layer must be split across masks, why EUV was worth its cost, and why design rules restrict pitches and orientations.

## Diffraction and the Rayleigh relation

A periodic mask of pitch $p$ diffracts light into orders at angles with $\sin\theta = m\lambda/p$. The lens collects angles up to its numerical aperture $NA = n \sin\theta_{max}$. An image forms only if at least two orders pass, so the lens acts as a low-pass filter on the mask's spatial frequencies. The smallest printable half-pitch is written $R = k_1 \lambda / NA$, where $k_1$ absorbs illumination, resist and process quality. For a 193 nm immersion scanner at NA 1.35 and $k_1 = 0.3$: $R = 0.3 \times 193/1.35 = 42.9$ nm, so the densest single-exposure line pitch is about 86 nm.

## The k1 a pitch demands

Turning the relation around tells how hard a pattern is: $k_1 = R \cdot NA / \lambda$. A 76 nm pitch on 193 nm immersion is a half-pitch of 38 nm, so $k_1 = 38 \times 1.35/193 = 0.266$. Production comfort lives around 0.35 to 0.4; below about 0.3 a layer needs strong resolution enhancement, restricted layouts and careful OPC. The hard floor is 0.25: with two-beam imaging the zeroth and one first order can at best sit at opposite edges of the pupil, giving a minimum pitch of $\lambda/(2NA)$. No mask trick prints a denser grating in one exposure, which is why multiple patterning exists.

## Wavelength and numerical aperture as levers

The other two levers are hardware. Wavelength fell from 365 nm (i-line) to 248 nm (KrF) to 193 nm (ArF), and then to 13.5 nm for EUV. NA rose until dry lenses neared 0.93; immersion in water, with index about 1.44, pushed it to 1.35. To print a 40 nm half-pitch at $k_1 = 0.35$ with 193 nm light needs $NA = 0.35 \times 193/40 = 1.69$, beyond any water-immersion lens; at 13.5 nm it needs only 0.12. Each lever has a price: shorter wavelengths need new sources, masks and resists, and higher NA costs depth of focus, which shrinks as $1/NA^2$.

## Going deeper

Mack, "Fundamental Principles of Optical Lithography: The Science of Microfabrication" (2007), chapters 2 and 3; Wong, "Resolution Enhancement Techniques in Optical Lithography".

label: Depth of focus and the focus budget
lesson:
# Depth of focus and the focus budget

A pattern prints correctly only within a narrow range of focus. That range, the depth of focus, shrinks as numerical aperture rises, and everything that moves the wafer surface out of the focal plane must fit inside it: wafer flatness, leftover topography from polishing, and the scanner's own focus control. Density and fill rules in a PDK are one way this budget reaches layout.

## The depth-of-focus relation

The usable focus range for a given feature is usually written $DOF = k_2 \lambda / NA^2$, where $k_2$ depends on the feature, the illumination and how much dose and size error is tolerated. For 193 nm immersion at NA 1.35 with $k_2 = 0.7$: $DOF = 0.7 \times 193 / 1.8225 = 74.1$ nm. For EUV at NA 0.33 with the same $k_2$: $0.7 \times 13.5 / 0.1089 = 86.8$ nm. A process window is the region in dose and focus where the printed size stays within specification; its focus extent at acceptable dose latitude is the working depth of focus.

## The price of numerical aperture

Resolution improves as $1/NA$ but depth of focus shrinks as $1/NA^2$. Raising NA from 0.33 to 0.55 at 13.5 nm improves resolution by a factor of 1.67 but cuts depth of focus by $(0.55/0.33)^2 = 2.78$. The same trade appeared when dry ArF moved from NA 0.75 to 0.93: resolution improved 24% while depth of focus fell by a factor of 1.54. High-NA EUV therefore needs thinner resists, flatter wafers and tighter focus control, and it is one reason design teams cannot assume a new tool solves a pitch without side effects.

## Budgeting focus

The depth of focus is a budget shared by every source of height error across the exposure field: wafer and chuck flatness, scanner focus and levelling errors, lens field curvature, and the topography left on the wafer by earlier steps. If a layer has 90 nm of usable depth of focus, flatness takes 20 nm and focus control takes 25 nm, the underlying topography may use at most 45 nm. That remainder is a requirement on CMP, and CMP's result depends on pattern density, so it becomes density rules and dummy fill in the PDK. A tool that places fill or routes metal is, indirectly, managing the lithographer's focus budget.

## Going deeper

Mack, "Fundamental Principles of Optical Lithography", chapters on focus and process windows; Burn J. Lin's papers on depth of focus scaling.

label: Photomasks, reduction and MEEF
lesson:
# Photomasks, reduction and MEEF

A photomask, or reticle, is a quartz plate carrying the pattern of one layer, written by an electron-beam or laser writer. Scanners image it at a reduction, so mask errors shrink on the wafer, but near the resolution limit they can be amplified again. Masks are a large share of the cost of a new design, and their geometry fixes how many dies one exposure prints.

## Reduction and mask scale

Modern scanners demagnify the mask by 4. A 20 nm wafer line is drawn as 80 nm on the mask before OPC bias, and a full scanner field of 26 mm by 33 mm on the wafer is 104 mm by 132 mm on a 6-inch mask. Reduction relaxes mask making: the mask writer works at four times the wafer dimension, and mask defects and size errors are divided by four in the image. DUV masks are chrome on quartz, often with an attenuating phase-shift film; EUV masks are reflective multilayer mirrors of molybdenum and silicon with an absorber pattern, used at a small angle of incidence.

## The mask error enhancement factor

Near the resolution limit the image does not respond linearly to mask changes. The mask error enhancement factor (MEEF) measures the amplification: $\Delta CD_{wafer} = MEEF \cdot \Delta CD_{mask}/M$, where $M = 4$ is the reduction. A MEEF of 1 means errors simply shrink by four. Dense lines at low $k_1$, contacts and line ends commonly have MEEF of 2 to 4. A 2 nm mask-scale error with MEEF 3 prints a $3 \times 2/4 = 1.5$ nm wafer error, three times what reduction alone predicts. High MEEF forces tighter mask specifications and makes OPC solutions more sensitive.

## Fields, dies and mask cost

One exposure prints one field; the scanner steps it across the wafer. A full field is 26 mm by 33 mm. A die of 12 mm by 15 mm fits $\lfloor 26/12 \rfloor \times \lfloor 33/15 \rfloor = 2 \times 2 = 4$ times per field. High-NA EUV uses anamorphic optics with 4x reduction in one direction and 8x in the other, so the field halves to 26 mm by 16.5 mm; a die taller than 16.5 mm then needs stitching across two exposures, which reaches the floorplanner. A leading-edge mask set has dozens of masks, so mask cost is a design-scale concern and a reason DTCO counts masks.

## Going deeper

Rizvi (ed.), "Handbook of Photomask Manufacturing Technology"; Wong, "Resolution Enhancement Techniques in Optical Lithography", on MEEF.

problems.q: A scanner projects the mask at 4x reduction. A line must print 30 nm wide on the wafer. How wide is it on the mask, in nanometres (ignoring OPC bias)?
problems.e: Mask dimensions are 4 times wafer dimensions: 120 nm.

problems.e: $\lfloor 26/18 \rfloor \times \lfloor 33/31 \rfloor = 1 \times 1 = 1$ dies per exposure.

label: Resolution enhancement techniques
prereqs: Depth of focus and the focus budget
lesson:
# Resolution enhancement techniques

At low $k_1$ an ordinary mask under ordinary illumination prints a blurred, low-contrast image. Resolution enhancement techniques (RET) change the illumination, the mask's phase and the mask's surroundings so that the image of the intended patterns improves. They shape layout in turn: RET tuned for a few pitches and orientations is why modern design rules are gridded, unidirectional and full of forbidden pitches.

## Off-axis illumination and phase shifting

With on-axis illumination, a grating images only if both first diffraction orders enter the lens. Tilting the illumination (annular, quadrupole or dipole sources) lets the zeroth order and one first order both pass at about half that pitch, which is how $k_1$ approaches its two-beam floor of 0.25. A dipole aligned to a grating images that orientation very well and the perpendicular one poorly, pushing critical metal layers to be unidirectional. Phase-shift masks add a 180-degree phase to some light: attenuated PSM leaks weak, phase-reversed light through dark areas to steepen edges, and alternating PSM gives neighbouring openings opposite phase.

## Assist features and source-mask optimization

An isolated line diffracts differently from a dense one, so it has a different best focus and size, the iso-dense bias. Sub-resolution assist features (SRAFs) are mask shapes too small to print that, placed beside an isolated line, make its diffraction pattern resemble a dense one. They need room: some spacings leave no space for an assist and print poorly. Source-mask optimization (SMO) treats the illumination pixels and the mask shapes as joint variables, optimized on a set of critical clips; the chosen source is then frozen and full-chip OPC runs against it.

## How RET constrains layout

RET is tuned for the patterns that matter most, so other patterns suffer. Strong off-axis illumination can leave forbidden pitches between the dense and isolated cases where contrast collapses. Alternating phase masks require a two-colouring of phase regions, and odd cycles in the conflict graph are unprintable without a layout change. The foundry's response is restricted design rules: a small set of allowed pitches, one direction per layer, fixed line widths and end-of-line rules. Those restrictions simplify the router's world but take away jogs and arbitrary spacing, and they explain many entries in the design-rule manual.

## Going deeper

Wong, "Resolution Enhancement Techniques in Optical Lithography" (2001); Rosenbluth et al., "Optimum mask and source patterns to print a given shape", Journal of Microlithography, Microfabrication and Microsystems (2002).

label: Optical proximity correction
lesson:
# Optical proximity correction

The image of a drawn rectangle is not a rectangle: corners round, line ends pull back, and widths shift with their neighbours. Optical proximity correction pre-distorts the mask so the printed shape lands on target. It is one of the largest compute jobs in the whole design-to-silicon chain and the main reason mask data looks nothing like the layout.

## Why printed shapes differ from drawn ones

The projection lens passes only low spatial frequencies, so sharp features blur. Corners lose intensity because they have neighbours on fewer sides, so they round. Line ends shorten, because the end of a line receives light from only one side. A line's printed width depends on what lies within the optical interaction range of a few hundred nanometres, so identical drawn lines print differently in dense and sparse contexts. Resist and etch add their own biases. Without correction, a gate drawn at 20 nm could print several nanometres off, and a line end could pull back enough to miss its via.

## Rule-based and model-based OPC

Rule-based OPC applies table-driven fixes: bias each edge by an amount that depends on its width and its space to the neighbour, add hammerheads to line ends and serifs to corners. It is fast but cannot capture complex two-dimensional context. Model-based OPC fragments each edge into short segments, simulates the aerial image and resist response with a calibrated compact model at a control site on each fragment, measures the edge placement error (EPE, printed minus target position), and moves the fragments to reduce it. It iterates until EPE is within tolerance. After correction, a verification run simulates the result across dose and focus to find hotspots that pinch or bridge.

## Inverse lithography and cost

Inverse lithography technology (ILT) poses the mask as the unknown of an optimization: find the mask pixels whose simulated print best matches the target across a process window. The solution includes assist features naturally and is often curvilinear. It gives better process window than fragment-moving OPC but costs far more compute, and curvilinear masks were slow on shaped-beam writers. GPUs and multi-beam writers have moved ILT from hotspots and memory arrays toward wider use. For design, OPC means context dependence: the same cell prints differently in different placements, and regular layouts reduce that spread.

## Going deeper

Cobb, "Fast Optical and Process Proximity Correction Algorithms for Integrated Circuit Manufacturing" (PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1998); Ma and Arce, "Computational Lithography" (2010).

lesson:
# Model-based OPC iteration

Model-based OPC is a numerical loop: simulate the print, measure edge placement errors, move mask fragments, repeat. Whether it converges, how fast, and how its errors are summarized are questions of fixed-point iteration. A tool designer who builds or tunes OPC engines decides the fragmentation, the feedback gain and the stopping rule, and those choices set runtime and quality across billions of fragments.

## Measuring edge placement error

Each fragment has a control site. The simulator computes the printed contour there, and the edge placement error is printed position minus target position, signed so that positive means the print lies outside the target. A polygon's quality is summarized by statistics over its fragments. For EPEs of 3, -2, 5 and -4 nm, the sum of squares is $9 + 4 + 25 + 16 = 54$, so the RMS EPE is $\sqrt{54/4} = 3.67$ nm, and the maximum magnitude is 5 nm. Both matter: RMS tracks overall fidelity, but a single bad fragment can still cause a bridge or an open, so tools also stop on maximum EPE.

## A feedback update for each fragment

Near its current position, moving a fragment by $b$ nm (at wafer scale) moves the printed edge by about $g b$, where $g$ is a local gain related to MEEF. OPC updates each fragment by $-f \cdot EPE$, with damping factor $f$. The new error is $EPE_{k+1} = EPE_k + g(-f\, EPE_k) = EPE_k(1 - f g)$. With $EPE_0 = 8$ nm, $g = 1.2$ and $f = 0.5$, the factor is $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$ and the error becomes 3.2 nm. If $f g = 1$ the correction is exact in one step; if $f g > 2$ the update overshoots and diverges.

## Convergence and stopping

The update is a fixed-point iteration with contraction factor $r = |1 - f g|$, so $|EPE_n| = r^n |EPE_0|$. The number of iterations to reach tolerance $\epsilon$ is the smallest $n$ with $r^n |EPE_0| \le \epsilon$. From 12 nm with $r = 0.4$ and $\epsilon = 0.5$ nm: 4.8, 1.92, 0.77, 0.31, so 4 iterations. In practice the gain differs by fragment and neighbouring fragments interact, so engines use conservative damping, per-fragment gains, and caps on iteration count. Each iteration re-simulates the image near every fragment, so cutting one iteration saves a large fraction of full-chip OPC runtime.

## Going deeper

Cobb, "Fast Optical and Process Proximity Correction Algorithms" (1998); Burden and Faires, "Numerical Analysis", the chapter on fixed-point iteration.

lesson:
# Extreme ultraviolet lithography

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses 13.5 nm light, about fourteen times shorter than ArF, so one exposure prints pitches that 193 nm immersion needs three or four masks to reach. It needs reflective optics in vacuum and reflective masks, and its small number of high-energy photons makes randomness a first-order effect. For design, EUV changes mask counts, rule complexity and the variability models for the tightest layers.

## Resolution at 13.5 nm

Every optic for 13.5 nm is a multilayer mirror, because no material is transparent at this wavelength, and the whole path runs in vacuum. Production tools have NA 0.33; high-NA tools have NA 0.55. With $k_1 = 0.4$, NA 0.33 prints a half-pitch of $0.4 \times 13.5/0.33 = 16.4$ nm, against $0.4 \times 193/1.35 = 57.2$ nm for 193 nm immersion. At NA 0.55 the same $k_1$ gives 9.8 nm. EUV masks are reflective, illuminated at about six degrees off normal, which introduces shadowing and mask three-dimensional effects that OPC must model.

## What a single EUV exposure replaces

The value of EUV is counted in masks avoided. If 193 nm immersion runs at $k_1 = 0.3$, its single-exposure pitch is $2 \times 0.3 \times 193/1.35 = 85.8$ nm. A layer at 36 nm pitch would need $\lceil 85.8/36 \rceil = 3$ litho-etch exposures with 193 nm light, or SAQP, against one EUV exposure. Fewer masks mean fewer overlay errors between masks, shorter cycle time and simpler colour-aware rules. EUV exposures are expensive, so the comparison is a cost and yield calculation, and at the tightest pitches EUV itself may be double patterned.

## Photon shot noise

An EUV photon carries $hc/\lambda \approx 91.8$ eV, about 14 times an ArF photon, so a given dose delivers 14 times fewer photons. At 30 mJ/cm^2, photons per square nanometre are $0.03\ \mathrm{J/cm^2} / 10^{14}\ \mathrm{nm^2/cm^2} / 1.47 \times 10^{-17}\ \mathrm{J} = 20.4$. A 10 nm by 10 nm pixel receives about 2040 photons, and as a Poisson count its relative fluctuation is $1/\sqrt{2040} = 2.2\%$. These stochastics cause line-edge roughness, missing or merged contacts and random micro-bridges, failures that a simple critical-dimension rule cannot describe. Raising dose reduces them but lowers scanner throughput.

## Going deeper

label: Multiple patterning
lesson:
# Multiple patterning

When a layer's pitch is below what one exposure can resolve, the pattern is split across several masks, each printing a sparser subset, and the results are combined on the wafer. Litho-etch-litho-etch (LELE) and its triple and quadruple variants split by assigning shapes to masks; self-aligned methods split by spacer deposition. For a tool designer, multiple patterning means coloured layouts, colour-aware rules and mask counts that DTCO has to price.

## Pitch splitting

In LELE, the first exposure and etch print every other line into a hard mask, and the second prints the lines in between. Each mask sees twice the final pitch. With $n$ litho-etch steps and lines assigned in rotation, each mask prints a pitch of $n p$. A 40 nm pitch split three ways asks each mask for 120 nm. The final pattern depends on overlay between the exposures: an overlay error shifts one set of lines relative to the other and changes alternate spaces, which is why same-mask and different-mask spacings are separate rules and why critical dimensions on multiple-patterned layers carry extra variation.

## How many exposures a pitch needs

A single exposure resolves a minimum pitch $P_{min} = 2 k_1 \lambda/NA$. To print pitch $p$ by splitting into $n$ masks, each mask's pitch $n p$ must be at least $P_{min}$, so $n = \lceil P_{min}/p \rceil$. For 193 nm immersion at NA 1.35 and $k_1 = 0.28$, $P_{min} = 80.1$ nm. A 64 nm pitch gives $80.1/64 = 1.25$ and needs 2 exposures; a 40 nm pitch gives $80.1/40 = 2.003$ and needs 3. Near such boundaries a small improvement in $k_1$ saves a whole mask, which is the sort of trade a DTCO study makes.

## Counting masks

Mask count drives cost and cycle time. Single exposure costs one mask per layer; LELE two; LELELE three. Self-aligned double or quadruple patterning needs one mandrel mask but usually one or more cut or block masks to remove unwanted line segments. A module with M1 by SADP plus two cut masks (3), M2 by LELE (2), V1 by LELELE (3) and M3 by single exposure (1) needs 9 masks for four layers. Counting masks per layer and per module lets a designer see why foundries pushed EUV, why unidirectional, gridded metal with cuts became standard, and why removing a single routing layer can matter in cost.

## Going deeper

label: Layout decomposition as graph coloring
lesson:
# Layout decomposition as graph coloring

To print a layer with several masks, every shape must be assigned to one mask so that shapes too close for one mask land on different masks. This is graph coloring: shapes are vertices, too-close pairs are edges, masks are colours. Decomposition engines in physical verification and colour-aware routers solve it, and its failures, odd cycles and dense clusters, show up as native conflicts that the layout must fix.

## Building the conflict graph

Every pair of shapes whose separation is below the same-mask minimum spacing $d$ becomes an edge of the conflict graph. Separation means the distance a mask can resolve: edge to edge for wires, centre to centre for small vias. Edges can join non-neighbours. Vias at positions 0, 30, 70 and 90 nm with $d = 50$ nm give edges (0, 30), (30, 70) and (70, 90), at distances 30, 40 and 20 nm; the pairs (0, 70), (0, 90) and (30, 90) are 70, 90 and 60 nm apart and do not conflict. The graph has three edges. Building the graph efficiently uses spatial indices or a sweep so that only nearby pairs are tested.

## Masks as colours

A decomposition with $k$ masks is a proper $k$-colouring of the conflict graph, so the fewest masks needed is the chromatic number. Two masks suffice exactly when the graph is bipartite, meaning it has no odd cycle. Three shapes that all conflict with each other form a triangle and need three masks; four mutually conflicting shapes need four. Two-colourability is checkable in linear time by breadth-first search, but deciding three-colourability is NP-complete, so triple-patterning decomposers use heuristics, integer programming or SAT on the small components that remain after splitting the graph into connected pieces.

## Native conflicts and stitches

When a graph is not two-colourable but the layer is LELE, some edges must remain inside one mask, and each is a violation to fix. The fewest such edges is found by choosing the best two-colouring, which is a maximum-cut problem. A wire can sometimes be split into two pieces on different masks with a small overlap, a stitch, which breaks an odd cycle at the cost of a yield-sensitive overlap region. Otherwise the layout must change: spread the shapes or reroute. Colour-aware routers and placers avoid creating odd cycles in the first place, which is cheaper than fixing them after the fact.

label: Self-aligned double and quadruple patterning
lesson:
# Self-aligned double and quadruple patterning

Self-aligned patterning halves the pitch without a second critical exposure. Mandrel lines are printed at a relaxed pitch, a conformal spacer film is deposited and etched back, and the mandrels are removed, leaving two spacer lines per mandrel. Repeat once more and the pitch quarters. The line width is set by film thickness rather than lithography, which gives excellent uniformity but imposes a gridded, unidirectional layout with separate cut masks.

## From mandrel to spacer lines

Print mandrels at pitch $P$. Deposit a conformal film of thickness $s$ by ALD or CVD and etch it anisotropically so only sidewall spacers remain. Remove the mandrels. Each mandrel leaves two spacers, so the spacer pitch is $P/2$: an 80 nm mandrel pitch gives 40 nm. SAQP repeats the process on the first spacers, giving $P/4$, so a 128 nm mandrel pitch becomes 32 nm. In the spacer-is-line flavour the spacers become the final lines, with width $s$. Because a deposited film is uniform to a fraction of a nanometre, line width varies far less than in litho-etch patterning.

## Alternating spaces

After mandrel removal, two kinds of gap alternate. Where a mandrel stood, the gap equals the mandrel width $m$. Between spacers of neighbouring mandrels, the gap is $P - m - 2s$. With $P = 96$ nm, $m = 30$ nm and $s = 16$ nm: the first gap is 30 nm and the second is $96 - 30 - 32 = 34$ nm. The two gaps come from different physical causes, mandrel lithography and etch for one, mandrel pitch and spacer thickness for the other, so they vary independently. Extraction and timing must treat the two spaces as two populations.

## Pitch walk and cut masks

Equal spaces require $m = P - m - 2s$, so the ideal mandrel width is $m = P/2 - s$: 32 nm for the example above. Any error in printed mandrel width makes line-to-line pitches alternate, $m + s$ across a mandrel and $P - m - s$ between mandrels, and their difference $|2m + 2s - P|$ is the pitch walk. A 4 nm mandrel error gives 8 nm of pitch walk. SADP also produces only continuous parallel lines, so line ends, gaps and jogs need separate cut or block masks, and those cuts carry their own rules on size, spacing and alignment. That is why SADP metal layers are fully gridded and unidirectional, and why routers for them reason about cut placement.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Mask data preparation

Between tapeout and a finished mask, the layout is transformed several times: layers are derived, corrected, verified, broken into writer primitives and written. This mask data preparation (MDP) chain decides whether the mask can be made, how long it takes to write, and whether a layout's hierarchy survives. Each step is a geometric engine with its own data structures and cost.

## The data path from tapeout to mask

Tapeout delivers drawn layers. Boolean and sizing operations derive the mask layers: a cut mask from line ends, implant masks from device layers, separate colours for multiple patterning. RET and OPC then correct each critical layer, and lithography verification simulates the result. Mask rule check (MRC) enforces the mask shop's own limits on minimum width, space and jog size, so OPC does not create slivers the mask writer cannot reproduce. Mask process correction (MPC) pre-compensates the mask writer's and mask etch's distortions. Finally the data is fractured into the writer's format and written, then inspected and repaired.

## Fracturing and shot count

A variable-shaped-beam (VSB) electron-beam writer exposes one rectangle or trapezoid per shot, up to a maximum size. Fracturing decomposes each post-OPC polygon into such primitives, a rectilinear polygon decomposition, and the write time grows with the number of shots. A rectangle $w$ by $h$ with maximum shot size $S$ needs $\lceil w/S \rceil \lceil h/S \rceil$ shots. An L-shaped polygon fractured into 1200 by 400 nm and 300 by 900 nm pieces with $S = 500$ nm needs $3 \times 1 + 1 \times 2 = 5$ shots. OPC jogs multiply rectangle counts, and curves multiply them again, which is why curvilinear masks were impractical on VSB writers.

## Data volume, hierarchy and multi-beam writing

OPC breaks hierarchy: identical cells in different contexts receive different corrections, so instances diverge and data grows. MDP tools exploit hierarchy where context repeats and flatten where it does not. Post-OPC files for a critical layer are far larger than the drawn layout. Multi-beam mask writers expose the mask with many thousands of beamlets in a raster, so write time depends on area and pixel size rather than on shape count, which finally made curvilinear ILT masks practical at full-chip scale. For a tool designer, MDP is a lesson in where geometry engines meet physical throughput limits.

## Going deeper

Rizvi (ed.), "Handbook of Photomask Manufacturing Technology"; the SEMI P39 OASIS specification for post-OPC data formats.

lesson:
# Process integration: FEOL, MOL and BEOL

Process integration is the art of ordering hundreds of unit steps so that each one leaves the wafer in a state the next can use. Foundries and designers divide the result into three segments: the front end builds devices, the middle of line connects to them, and the back end wires them together. Each segment has its own materials, rules, models and failure modes, and each maps to different engines in a design flow.

## Three segments of the flow

The front end of line (FEOL) forms the transistors: shallow trench isolation, wells, fins or nanosheet stacks, the gate stack, spacers, and epitaxial source and drain. The middle of line (MOL) forms the local contacts: trench contacts to source and drain, the gate contact, and the first via level, often called V0, that reaches the first metal. The back end of line (BEOL) is the stack of copper or other metal wiring levels separated by low-k dielectric and joined by vias, ending in thick top metals and pads. Thermal budget enforces the order: FEOL steps reach about 1000 C, while once silicides and copper exist the flow must stay near 400 C.

## Why the middle of line became its own segment

At older nodes, contacts were a single small step between devices and metal 1. As gate pitch shrank, the space between gate and contact became a few nanometres, and contact resistance became a large share of a transistor's total resistance. The MOL gained its own materials (cobalt or tungsten fills, thin liners), self-aligned processes that use the gate cap as an etch stop, and its own rules. Contact over active gate (COAG) lets the gate contact land above the channel region rather than on isolation, removing a constraint on cell height. For tools, MOL parasitics are now first-order inputs to cell characterization and extraction.

## Consequences for design tools

The segments map onto the flow. FEOL and MOL shapes are mostly fixed inside library cells and drawn by layout engineers or generators; BEOL shapes are drawn by routers. Overlay error between a via and the line below is a large fraction of spacing at tight pitch, so self-aligned via processes use the line trench to confine the via, which in turn changes via rules. Changing an MOL dielectric thickness changes gate-to-contact capacitance and therefore every cell's timing. Moving power delivery to the wafer back removes the power network from the front-side BEOL. Knowing which segment a change touches tells a tool designer which models and rules must be regenerated.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology", chapter 11 on process integration; the IEEE IRDS "More Moore" roadmap chapters on interconnect and device integration.

lesson:
# The interconnect stack

Above the transistors sit ten to twenty wiring levels. The lowest are thin, dense and resistive, for local connections inside and between cells; higher levels are progressively wider and thicker, for long routes, clocks and power. The stack's pitches and directions define the routing resource every placer and router reasons about, and its cross-sections set the resistance and capacitance that timing sees.

## Layers, pitches and directions

Each metal layer has a pitch, a preferred direction and a thickness. Adjacent layers alternate horizontal and vertical so that a route can turn by dropping through one via. Layers are grouped by pitch: the tightest local layers (often called 1x) near the cells, then intermediate and semi-global layers at two or four times that pitch, then thick global layers for power and clock. The number of routing tracks a layer supplies across a block is the block dimension divided by the pitch: a 40 um wide block on a vertical layer at 32 nm pitch offers $\lfloor 40000/32 \rfloor = 1250$ tracks.

## Routing supply across the stack

A router's capacity model counts tracks per layer, per direction, per region. Horizontal layers supply tracks across the block's height; vertical layers across its width. For a 20 um by 30 um block with M2 horizontal at 28 nm, M3 vertical at 36 nm and M4 horizontal at 40 nm, supply is $\lfloor 30000/28 \rfloor + \lfloor 20000/36 \rfloor + \lfloor 30000/40 \rfloor = 1071 + 555 + 750 = 2376$ tracks. Some of that supply is consumed by power rails, straps, pin access and blockages, so routers work with effective capacity. Global routers divide the block into tiles and compare demand against these per-tile capacities to estimate congestion.

## Why long wires go up

At fixed aspect ratio and width equal to half the pitch, the wire cross-section scales with pitch squared, so resistance per unit length scales as $1/p^2$. A 24 nm pitch layer has $(96/24)^2 = 16$ times the resistance per length of a 96 nm pitch layer. Capacitance per length changes far less because it depends on ratios of dimensions. Long routes therefore belong on upper layers, at the cost of via stacks to reach them and of fewer tracks. Layer assignment, deciding which nets use which layers, is a timing-driven optimization in routers and in buffering, and the stack definition in the PDK's technology files is its input.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters on global routing; the IRDS interconnect tables for typical stack pitches.

lesson:
# Damascene copper and barriers

Copper cannot be plasma-etched cleanly, so copper wires are made by damascene: etch trenches and via holes in dielectric, line them with a barrier, fill with copper, and polish the excess away. The barrier keeps copper from diffusing into the dielectric and silicon, but it is poorly conducting and does not scale down with the wire, so it takes an ever larger share of the cross-section. That share is a direct input to wire resistance in extraction.

## The dual-damascene sequence

In dual damascene, one level's via holes and line trenches are both etched into the dielectric, in a via-first or trench-first order. A thin barrier, typically tantalum nitride with a tantalum or cobalt liner, is deposited by PVD or ALD, then a copper seed by PVD. Electroplating fills trench and via together from the bottom up. CMP removes the copper and barrier overburden from the field and leaves copper only in the trenches, flush with the dielectric. A dielectric cap then seals the top. Because filling and polishing define the line, CMP dishing and erosion directly change line thickness, which is why metal density rules exist.

## Copper area after the barrier

The barrier lines both sidewalls and the bottom. For a trench of width $w$ and height $h$ with barrier thickness $b$, copper occupies $(w - 2b)(h - b)$. A 24 nm by 48 nm trench with 3 nm barrier holds $18 \times 45 = 810$ nm^2 of copper out of 1152, which is 70.3%. With copper resistivity 5 micro-ohm cm (50 ohm nm, including size effects) and negligible barrier current, resistance per micrometre is $50 \times 1000/810 = 61.7$ ohm. Note that 1 micro-ohm cm equals 10 ohm nm, a conversion worth memorizing.

## A barrier that does not scale

At the same copper resistivity, the barrier raises resistance by $A_{trench}/A_{Cu}$: $1152/810 = 1.42$ in the example. Halve both dimensions to 12 nm by 24 nm with the same 3 nm barrier, and copper is $6 \times 21 = 126$ nm^2 of 288, a factor of 2.29. Copper's resistivity also rises sharply in narrow lines from surface and grain-boundary scattering. Together these effects explain why foundries study thinner barriers, barrier-free metals such as ruthenium or molybdenum, and alternative schemes such as subtractive etch for the tightest layers, and why extraction tools use width-dependent resistivity tables rather than a single bulk value.

## Going deeper

Andricacos et al., "Damascene copper electroplating for chip interconnections", IBM Journal of Research and Development (1998); Gall, "The search for the most conductive metal for narrow interconnect lines", Journal of Applied Physics (2020).

label: Wire RC per unit length and scaling
lesson:
# Wire RC per unit length and scaling

Every routed net is, electrically, a distributed resistance and capacitance. Resistance per unit length comes from resistivity and cross-section; capacitance per unit length from geometry and dielectric. Their product sets how wire delay grows with length, and its behaviour under scaling is why interconnect, not transistors, often limits performance at advanced nodes.

## Resistance per unit length

A rectangular wire of width $w$ and thickness $t$ with resistivity $\rho$ has resistance per length $r = \rho/(w t)$. With $\rho = 4$ micro-ohm cm (40 ohm nm), $w = 20$ nm and $t = 40$ nm: $r = 40 \times 1000/800 = 50$ ohm per um. For narrow copper, $\rho$ is an effective value well above the bulk 1.7 micro-ohm cm because electrons scatter at surfaces and grain boundaries, and the barrier steals cross-section. Extraction rule files therefore tabulate resistance against drawn width and sometimes spacing. Capacitance per length, typically 0.1 to 0.25 fF/um for local wires, comes from area and fringe coupling to the layers above and below and to neighbours on the same layer.

## Distributed RC delay

A uniform line of length $L$ with $r$ and $c$ per unit length has total resistance $rL$ and capacitance $cL$, but each piece of capacitance sees only the resistance between it and the driver. The Elmore delay of the distributed line is $r c L^2/2$. For $r = 50$ ohm/um, $c = 0.2$ fF/um and $L = 200$ um: $0.5 \times 50 \times 0.2 \times 40000 = 200{,}000$ ohm fF, which is 200 ps. The square law means doubling length quadruples delay, which is why long wires are broken by repeaters: with optimal buffering, delay grows linearly in length.

## What scaling does to wires

Shrink width and thickness by a factor $s < 1$. Resistance per length rises by $1/s^2$; capacitance per length stays roughly constant because it depends on ratios of dimensions. A route of fixed length therefore gets slower by $1/s^2$, and more when size effects raise resistivity. With $s = 0.7$ and resistivity up by 1.2, a 20 ps route becomes $20 \times 1.2/0.49 = 49$ ps. Local wires shrink in length along with the cells, which partly compensates, but global wires do not. This is the interconnect bottleneck behind buffering, layer assignment, low-k dielectrics and backside power.

## Going deeper

Bakoglu, "Circuits, Interconnections, and Packaging for VLSI" (1990); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits", chapter 4.

# Low-k dielectrics and air gaps

Wire capacitance is proportional to the permittivity of the insulator around it. Replacing silicon dioxide, with relative dielectric constant about 3.9 to 4.2, by carbon-doped or porous films with $k$ near 2.5 to 3 cuts capacitance, delay and dynamic power. The cost is mechanical weakness and integration difficulty, and real stacks mix low-k films with higher-k caps and etch stops.

## Capacitance scales with k

At fixed geometry, every capacitance between conductors scales with the relative permittivity $k$ of the dielectric between them. A wire with 0.20 fF/um in oxide of $k = 4.0$ would have $0.20 \times 2.7/4.0 = 0.135$ fF/um in a $k = 2.7$ film. Since delay of a wire-dominated path is roughly proportional to $RC$ and dynamic power to $C V^2 f$, a lower $k$ helps both. Low-k films achieve it by adding carbon and hydrogen (SiCOH) to break up the polar Si-O network, and ultra-low-k films add porosity, since air has $k = 1$.

## Effective k of a real stack

Between two metal levels there is not one film but several: an etch-stop or copper cap of higher $k$, often 4.5 to 7, and the low-k bulk. For vertical coupling these act as capacitors in series, so $k_{eff} = (t_1 + t_2)/(t_1/k_1 + t_2/k_2)$. A 10 nm cap at $k = 5.5$ under 90 nm of low-k at $k = 2.6$ gives $100/(1.82 + 34.6) = 2.75$, higher than the bulk film. A thin high-k layer costs more than its thickness suggests. Lateral coupling between neighbours on the same layer sees mostly the low-k fill, plus any liner or damage layer on the trench sidewalls.

## Air gaps and the limits of low-k

Air gaps remove dielectric between closely spaced lines on selected layers, lowering the effective lateral $k$ toward 1. If a fraction $f$ of a wire's capacitance is lateral and the gap lowers lateral $k$ from $k$ to $k_g$, total capacitance falls by $f(1 - k_g/k)$. With $f = 0.6$, $k = 2.7$ and $k_g = 1.4$, the saving is $0.6 \times 0.48 = 28.9\%$. Porous and gapped films are mechanically weak, crack under packaging stress, absorb moisture and are damaged by plasma etch, which raises their $k$ again. Extraction must know where gaps exist, usually through layer-specific rules, and reliability rules limit where they can be used.

## Going deeper

Grill, Gates, Ryan, Nguyen and Priyadarshini, "Progress in the development and understanding of advanced low k and ultralow k dielectrics for very large-scale integrated interconnects", Applied Physics Reviews (2014).

# Contact and via resistance

Current enters a transistor through a contact to silicide on its source or drain and climbs to the wiring through a chain of vias. At advanced nodes these vertical connections contribute as much resistance as the transistor channel itself for short paths. Their values, and the effect of using several in parallel, feed cell characterization, extraction and power-grid analysis.

## Specific contact resistivity

The resistance of a metal-semiconductor interface scales inversely with its area: $R_c = \rho_c/A$, where $\rho_c$ is the specific contact resistivity in ohm cm^2. Good silicide contacts reach about $10^{-9}$ ohm cm^2. A contact interface of 20 nm by 20 nm has area 400 nm^2 $= 4 \times 10^{-12}$ cm^2, so $R_c = 10^{-9}/(4 \times 10^{-12}) = 250$ ohm. Halving the area doubles it. This is why contact area shrinkage hurts so much, why trench contacts run the full width of the active region, and why wrap-around contacts on epitaxial source-drain regions are attractive.

## Via stacks in series and parallel

A route from metal 1 to metal 6 crosses five via levels in series; each level may use one via or several in parallel. Total resistance is the sum over levels of $R_{via}/k$, where $k$ is the number of parallel vias at that level, ignoring the short metal landings. Levels of 40 ohm single, 30 ohm doubled and 20 ohm doubled give $40 + 15 + 10 = 65$ ohm. Lower vias are smaller and more resistive than upper ones. Power grids use arrays of vias for this reason, and DFM flows double single vias where space allows, which lowers both resistance and the probability of an open.

## When contacts dominate

For a short local connection, the path from one transistor to another may be two contacts, a few vias and a short wire. With 150 ohm contacts, 60 ohm of vias and 100 ohm of wire, contacts carry $300/460 = 65\%$ of the resistance. Wire length optimization cannot touch that share; only process changes (better silicide, larger contact area, new MOL metals) or architecture changes (fewer contacts in series, backside contacts) can. Timing extraction must therefore model MOL resistance in detail, and DTCO studies treat contact resistivity as a primary knob alongside pitch.

## Going deeper

Schroder, "Semiconductor Material and Device Characterization", chapter 3 on contact resistance; the IRDS interconnect chapter on via and contact resistance trends.

lesson:
# What a process design kit contains

A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's description of a process, packaged for design tools. It contains device models, rules, technology files, layer definitions and parameterized device layouts, versioned together. Every EDA engine is configured from it. For a tool designer, the PDK is the boundary between algorithm and process: code that hard-codes a process fact breaks on the next node.

## The pieces of a PDK

A typical PDK ships: SPICE-level device models (BSIM-CMG for FinFETs, with corners and statistical variants); a design-rule manual and signoff decks for DRC, LVS, antenna and density; extraction rule files describing layer thicknesses, permittivities and resistivities; a layer map assigning names and purposes to GDS layer and datatype numbers; technology files for layout editors and routers, such as technology LEF; and parameterized cells (PCells) that generate device layouts from width, length and finger count. Standard-cell libraries, memories and I/O are built on top of the PDK, usually as separate IP. Customer design data is never part of it.

## Which tool reads which file

Each engine reads its own slice. Circuit simulators read device models. Routers read technology LEF: layer directions, pitches, widths, via definitions and a subset of spacing rules. Extractors read the interconnect technology description. DRC and LVS engines read rule decks: the LVS deck also contains device recognition rules that extract transistors from layer combinations. Layout editors read the layer map and display settings. Because GDS stores only integers, a wrong layer map silently mislabels data, so every tool must use the same one. Open PDKs let researchers publish full flows on real processes, which closed PDKs under non-disclosure agreements do not.

## Versions and maturity

PDKs evolve. Early versions use projected rules and pre-silicon models; later releases re-fit models to silicon and adjust rules as yield learning progresses. A change of one spacing value can make a previously clean layout fail, so design teams record the PDK version with every result and re-run signoff after updates. For tool developers this means treating PDK content as configuration: the same engine must run many processes and versions, read process facts from files, and validate that the files it reads are consistent, for example that the router's abstract rules agree with the signoff deck.

## Going deeper

The SkyWater SKY130 and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU open PDK documentation; the Si2 OpenPDK specifications.

lesson:
# Design rules

Design rules are geometric constraints a layout must satisfy so that it can be manufactured with acceptable yield: minimum widths, spacings, enclosures, extensions, areas and densities. Each one encodes a limit of some process step. Routers, placers and cell generators must obey them by construction, and DRC engines check them, so their arithmetic is part of every physical-design algorithm.

## Width, space and pitch

The simplest rules are a minimum width per layer and a minimum space between shapes on that layer. Their sum is the tightest pitch: a layer with 18 nm minimum width and 22 nm minimum space supports a 40 nm line pitch. Width rules protect against opens and lithography failure of thin lines; space rules protect against shorts and bridges. Rules are checked on the polygons, with Manhattan geometry for most layers, so a DRC engine measures edge-to-edge distances between parallel edges and corner-to-corner distances where shapes approach diagonally. Routers turn the same numbers into a track grid.

## Enclosure and via landing

Enclosure rules require one layer to extend past another: metal must surround a via by a margin $e$ so that overlay error and size variation never leave the via partly outside the metal. A via of size $v$ in a line therefore forces line width at least $v + 2e$ across the line. If vias are 16 nm, enclosure is 4 nm and line spacing is 20 nm, a layer whose every line must accept a via has pitch $16 + 8 + 20 = 44$ nm, not the 36 nm that minimum width alone might suggest. Line-end enclosure along the line direction is often larger than side enclosure, because line ends pull back in printing.

## Width-dependent and conditional spacing

Wide metal needs more space: it dishes more in CMP, carries more current and prints with different bias. Spacing tables therefore select the required space by the width of the wider wire, and often by parallel run length. With a table of 20 nm up to 60 nm width, 28 nm up to 150 nm, and 40 nm above, a 100 nm wire beside a 20 nm wire must be 28 nm away edge to edge, so their centres are at least $50 + 28 + 10 = 88$ nm apart. Routers model such rules when they place wide power and clock wires, and many violations in practice come from conditional rules that a simple width-and-space model misses.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design", chapter on design rules and physical verification; the SKY130 PDK design-rule documentation as a public example.

lesson:
# Design-rule manuals and rule decks

The design-rule manual (DRM) is the foundry's human-readable definition of every rule, with figures and conditions. The rule deck, or runset, is the executable form that a DRC engine runs. Modern nodes have thousands of rules, most of them conditional, and the gap between the manual's words and the deck's code is where many tool bugs and design surprises live.

## From simple numbers to conditional rules

Early processes needed a few dozen rules of the form "width at least $w$, space at least $s$". Advanced nodes add rules whose values depend on context: spacing that grows with parallel run length or wire width, end-of-line spacing for line tips facing other shapes, enclosure that depends on the direction of the line, minimum area and minimum enclosed area, colour-dependent spacing for multiple-patterned layers, antenna ratios limiting metal area connected to a gate during plasma processing, and density windows for CMP. Each condition encodes a process mechanism such as line-end pull-back, charging damage or polish dishing, so reading the mechanism is the fastest way to understand the rule.

## How a deck computes a check

A rule deck is a program in a geometric language. It derives layers by boolean and sizing operations (gate equals poly AND active), selects edges by orientation and context, measures distances between selected edges, and emits violation markers. An extension check for gate poly past active, for example, intersects the layers, takes the poly edges outside active, and measures them. Engines run these operations on polygon databases with spatial indices and sweeps, often hierarchically to reuse results for repeated cells. When the manual and the deck disagree, signoff follows the deck, and the discrepancy is reported to the foundry rather than edited locally.

## Recommended rules and restricted layouts

Beyond mandatory rules, many manuals list recommended rules: wider spaces, double vias, longer extensions. They are not required for signoff but raise yield, so DFM flows score and apply them where area and timing allow. Some hotspots depend on two-dimensional configurations that no width or space rule captures, so decks add pattern-matching rules from libraries of known-bad shapes. Gridded, unidirectional layers replace many of these rules with a few simple ones, at the cost of routing flexibility. For routers the lesson is direct: any rule the router does not model becomes a violation that a later repair loop must fix.

## Going deeper

The KLayout DRC scripting documentation and the Magic VLSI technology-file documentation, as open examples of rule-deck languages; Lienig and Scheible, "Fundamentals of Layout Design for Electronic Circuits" (2020).

lesson:
# Device models and corners in a PDK

A PDK's device models describe how each transistor behaves across voltage, temperature and process variation. Corners bound the global spread, statistical models describe mismatch, and layout-dependent parameters carry context. Every timing library, every circuit simulation and every power estimate is computed from these models, so their structure decides what margin a design must carry.

## Corners for global variation

Transistors vary from lot to lot and wafer to wafer. Foundries summarize this with process corners named by NMOS then PMOS speed: TT (typical), SS (slow-slow), FF (fast-fast), and the skewed SF and FS. Skewed corners matter for circuits that depend on the ratio of NMOS to PMOS strength, such as SRAM cells, level shifters and ratioed logic. Each corner is combined with supply voltage and temperature to define a PVT corner, and Liberty libraries are characterized at each. Slow corners at low voltage bound setup timing; fast corners at high voltage and temperature bound leakage and hold.

## Statistical models and mismatch

Corners stack worst cases and can be pessimistic, or miss combinations. Statistical models describe parameter distributions so Monte Carlo simulation can sample real behaviour. They separate global variation, shared by all devices on a die, from local mismatch between nominally identical neighbours, which comes from random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and work-function granularity. Pelgrom's law says mismatch standard deviation scales as $1/\sqrt{WL}$: quadrupling gate area halves mismatch sigma. Library characterization uses these models to produce variation-aware timing data, such as Liberty variation format tables. Those tables let a timer carry sigma per arc instead of a flat margin.

## Layout dependence, aging and model maturity

A transistor's threshold and mobility depend on its surroundings: distance to the well edge (well proximity effect), length of diffusion and distance to diffusion breaks (stress effects), and neighbouring gate density. Extraction measures these distances and passes them as instance parameters so simulation sees the layout context. Reliability models add end-of-life shifts from bias temperature instability and hot-carrier injection, which feed aging-aware timing margins. Device corners and interconnect RC corners are separate because FEOL and BEOL vary from different steps. Early models are projections and are re-fitted as silicon data arrives, so timing results carry the model version.

## Going deeper

label: Dies per wafer and edge loss
lesson:
# Dies per wafer and edge loss

How many dies a wafer holds is the denominator of every cost-per-die calculation and an input to yield and DTCO trade-offs. Rectangular dies do not tile a circle, so the count is less than wafer area over die area, and the loss is worst for large dies. A standard closed-form estimate captures the edge loss well enough for early studies, and exact counts come from placing the die grid.

## Area ratio as an upper bound

The crude estimate divides wafer area by die area. A 300 mm wafer has area $\pi \times 150^2 = 70{,}686$ mm^2. A 10 mm by 10 mm die gives a ratio of 706.9. That number is an upper bound: it counts fractional dies at the edge and ignores the area that partial dies waste. It is still useful as a sanity check, and the gap between it and the real count grows with die size because the wasted ring around the edge is roughly one die deep. Larger dies waste a deeper ring.

## The edge-loss formula

A widely used estimate subtracts a term for the edge: $DPW = \pi d^2/(4A) - \pi d/\sqrt{2A}$, with wafer diameter $d$ and die area $A$. The second term approximates the number of dies lost along the circumference: the circumference $\pi d$ divided by the die diagonal $\sqrt{2A}$. For $d = 300$ mm and $A = 100$ mm^2: $706.9 - 942.5/14.14 = 706.9 - 66.6 = 640.2$, so about 640 dies. For a 400 mm^2 die the area term is 176.7 and the edge term 33.3, leaving 143: edge loss is 19% for the large die against 9% for the small one.

## Edge exclusion, scribe lanes and exact counts

Two corrections matter in practice. The edge exclusion removes a ring of width $e$, so the usable diameter is $d - 2e$. Scribe lanes, the saw streets between dies that also carry test structures, enlarge the die pitch to $(w + s)(h + s)$. A 10 by 10 mm die with 0.1 mm scribe on a 300 mm wafer with 3 mm exclusion uses $d = 294$ and $A = 102.01$, giving $665.6 - 64.7 = 600$ dies. Exact counts come from placing the die grid and counting dies entirely inside the usable circle; tools also optimize the grid offset, which can gain several dies. Die aspect ratio matters too, which floorplanners can exploit.

## Going deeper
